title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6756 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: Finland Inflation Rises to 3.1% in October
body: Finland's annual inflation rate accelerated to 3.1% in October 2026, up from 2.5% in September, reaching its highest level since January 2024. The increase was largely driven by higher prices for food and non-alcoholic beverages (2.6% vs 1.9% in September), housing and utilities (3.0% vs 1.6%), and transport (9.6% vs 8.9%). Additional upward pressure came from recreation, sports and culture (1.8% vs 1.5%), furnishings, household equipment and routine household maintenance (3.1% vs 2.9%), and alcoholic beverages and tobacco (4.3% vs 3.8%). By contrast, inflation eased in information and communication (3.4% vs 4.5%), restaurants and accommodation services (1.8% vs 2.0%), and health (2.3% vs 2.5%), while education costs were unchanged at 4.2%. Price declines moderated for clothing and footwear (-0.6% vs -0.9%), but deepened for personal care, social protection, and miscellaneous goods and services (-2.0% vs -1.9%). On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose by 0.4% in October, slowing from a 0.7% increase in September. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: Goldman Sachs: We can explain almost the entire US inflation overshoot by tariffs and the war in Iran
body: Goldman Sachs is out with a chart that says the US inflation problem is almost entirely two things: tariffs and the Iran energy shock. Take those out and inflation is basically at target. The latest hard data is ugly. September PCE was 3.6% y/y on headline and 3.1% on core, with gasoline and other energy goods up 9.2% in the month alone. Goldman sees headline peaking just shy of 3.9% right about now and core topping out near 3.3%. Strip out the two shocks and the picture changes: Headline PCE ex-temporary drivers: roughly 2.2% Core PCE ex-temporary drivers: roughly 2.4% Energy/Iran is worth about 1.5 pp on headline at the peak Tariffs are worth another 0.3-0.4 pp on headline and were closer to a full point on core earlier this year Tariff effects are largely gone by mid-2027; the energy effect fades through late 2027 Headline is back near 2.1% and core near 2.4% by the end of 2027 That's the case for looking through it. Tariffs are a one-time level shift and oil doesn't rise 30% every year. Hiking rates doesn't reopen Hormuz. Here's the catch: Goldman's own economists don't think the Fed will look through it. After Tuesday's hot October CPI, the third straight upside surprise, they added a hike to their forecast. They now see 25 bps in December and another 25 bps in March, and they pushed the first cut back to December 2027. A month ago they were arguing the Fed might be one-and-done after September. The rest of the Street is moving faster.

title: Fed's Goolsbee: We're not on the way to 2% inflation and we have to deal with that
body: Inflation has spread into categories where prices not driven by energy The jobs market looks stable, if not tightening a bit Rates will eventually go well-below today We have had signs of trouble for several months in a row now Lately we're not making any progress and if anything, it's going the wrong way Inflation is rising and proving far more persistent than expected when it was just a matter of supply shocks The Fed "definitely has work to do" to maintain its credibility Services inflation and rising health care costs don't feel like they will change quickly Even if the price of oil goes down rapidly, refining capacity is still very problematic My feeling is that right now we're not on the way to 2% and we have to deal with that Demand-overheating inflation shocks are extremely hard to get rid of Until about six months ago I thought AI overheating was staying in its lane; I've begun to change that view The tariff and oil price shocks were supposed to have gone away by now This is the guy who used to be the most reliable dove on the FOMC. He's now talking about demand overheating and Fed credibility. He was pushed on 25 bps versus something faster in December and wouldn't bite, but he didn't push back on the premise either. He was also asked about Bessent's warning, which invoked the ECB hiking in 2008 right before the financial crisis. He was polite about it and then went straight back to inflation persistence. There's an out here.

We will hear from the Fed's Goolsbee on CNBC momentarily and he recently called inflation "borderline alarming". Ahead of the data, the market was pricing in 28.5 bps of hikes for December, which is a bit over a 10% chance of a 50 bps move, with 86 bps in hikes priced in over the coming year. For background, the Producer Price Index from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics measures the average change in prices that domestic producers receive for their goods, services and construction. It's released monthly at 8:30 am ET, typically a day or two after CPI, and tracks inflation from the seller's side rather than the consumer's. The headline is the final demand index, which covers output sold for personal consumption, business investment, government and export. Services make up about 68% of it, goods about 29% and construction the rest, so it's far broader than a gauge of factory-gate prices.

title: Crude oil jumps as escalation risks increase after Trump says the US doesn't need Iran deal
body: Crude oil jumped yesterday after Trump stated on Truth Social that the US does not need a deal with Iran, fuelling escalation concerns. Trump warned that the US would not hesitate to take further military action if current measures fail to achieve objectives, while CENTCOM is implementing the naval blockade and working to restore commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The reported US airstrikes on Sirik, followed by Iranian claims of retaliatory attacks against US radar infrastructure in Bahrain, show that the situation is becoming increasingly fragile. Iran warned that any country directly or indirectly participating in actions against its interests will be considered hostile and held responsible for the consequences. Moreover, there were reports of the Houthis attacking again Saudi energy infrastructure, including the East-West pipeline and Yanbu oil facility. The Saudi-Houthi conflict adds another layer of risk to energy disruptions, but the US-Iran standoff remains the main driver. It goes without saying that a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations would trigger a significant selloff and take oil prices back to pre-war levels relatively quickly. But as of now, this scenario looks much less probable. An escalation or a prolonged stalemate should keep oil prices supported, although there's also a chance that Trump decides to proceed with limited strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities before exiting the war.

But as mentioned with the release then, there is a bit of a catch when it comes to the relative resilience we're seeing here. Ireland is the standout in terms of growth numbers with a whopping 5.5% quarterly expansion in Q3. However, let's be reminded of the fact that Ireland has a knack for notoriously volatile GDP figures in the past year and that always warrants some caution. The expansion here was primarily driven by strong activity in multinational-dominated industries, specifically information and communication and manufacturing. For some context, Ireland's headline growth figure is often a distorted gauge of domestic economic health. That is because it is heavily influenced by contract manufacturing and global profits of multinational corporations that largely flow back to foreign shareholders rather than translating directly into local living standards. Looking to the bigger names, things aren't as great. Germany managed just 0.2% growth, Italy stagnated at 0.0%, and France even contracted by 0.1%.

title: Spain inflation remains stubborn in October, keeping ECB rate hike expectations firmly alive
body: Spain October final CPI +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y prelim Prior +4.9% Spain October final HICP +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y prelim Prior +5.0% Spain October core CPI +3.1% y/y Prior +3.1% No changes to the preliminary estimates as the final report here reaffirms that Spanish inflation remains stubborn with headline prices keeping near 5% in October. The latest drop in energy prices over the past week or so might help eventually but it will take some time to filter through to the economy. But for now, inflation pressures are at a rather uncomfortable level for Spain indubitably. Besides that, core annual inflation is reaffirmed at 3.1% in October and that is unchanged from September. Even so, it is still well above what the ECB would be comfortable with as price pressures continue to pull away from the 2% target. Alongside the French report from earlier, this just continues to reaffirm that the inflation monster is still a major threat that the ECB has to deal with heading into the final stages of this year. As things stand, markets are pricing in roughly 82% odds of the ECB making another move in December. For policymakers, they might very well have to go with the flow amid fears that flagging economic growth conditions could make their jobs much tougher come next year. In the grand scheme of things, it's not a good look for the ECB as they have quite a tough balancing act to work with. On the one hand, they have to deal with more persistent price pressures before they get out of control.

title: France October inflation accelerates as energy prices surge, keeping ECB rate hike bets alive
body: France October final CPI +3.4% vs +3.4% y/y prelim Prior +3.1% France October final HICP +3.7% vs +3.8% y/y prelim Prior +3.4% The final report here confirms a further acceleration in French inflation pressures to start the final quarter of the year. That owes much to another jump in energy prices, which climbed by another 1.9% on the month and are up by 24.1% compared to October last year. The annual estimate is once again after after the estimates for August and September of +16.7% and +21.3% respectively. That being said, core annual inflation also picked up in October in moving to 1.7% - up from 1.5% in September. That comes as services inflation continues to rise further as well, moving up to 2.6% in October - up from 2.4% in September and 1.9% in August. Ouch. With that, it reaffirms that price pressures in Europe's second-largest economy are continuing to intensify and at a rather awkward time. With French growth conditions struggling and fiscal risks mounting, it is making for a rather untimely backdrop for policymakers to be dealing with stronger inflation. As such, that will keep ECB policymakers on their toes in navigating the next steps. For now, the report here will just reinforce expectations of another rate hike in December with markets also pricing in roughly 82% odds of that at the moment. This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

title: The US consumer may be hitting a wall. A look at eight indicators
body: The old addage is: Never underestimate the spending power of the US consumer. That stance has been a remarkably good one for traders. Time after time, Americans have dug into their pockets and kept the economy churning. But never say never. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly was just out with a comment, highlighting that she's "just starting to hear the consumer may be running out of gas." Now that might not be a big red flag. In the Oct 14 Beige Book, the SF Fed reported: "Retail sales softened slightly. Contacts continued to describeeconomic conditions as bifurcated or K-shaped, with one contact observing that mounting financial pressures on lower-income families have spread to impact middle-income households." Now the K-shape is nothing new and in that same Beige Book, over half of the districts said spending was driven by high-income households. Still, with the election swinging on affordability, gasoline prices staying high and inflation biting, now would be a time to see cracks. In the week ahead, we will get earnings from Walmart, Target, Home Depot and others, so that will be the best check. We also get official Octobe retail sales, with economists seeing the closely-watched 'control group' up 0.4% m/m. This could be the week where Wall Street realizes that while it's been breathlessly watching AI and the Anthropic IPO, the foundations of the US economy have been eroding.

title: Earnings week ahead: Nvidia without Jensen, Anthropic's IPO, and the consumer meets a hiking Fed
body: Earnings season is supposed to be over. Instead, next week might be the most important of the quarter for the macro view. Nvidia reports days after losing its founder. Anthropic prices what could be the largest equity deal ever. And every major US retailer reports into a rate-hike cycle. October CPI came in hot at 0.4% headline and 0.3% core, a December hike is fully priced with a 12% chance of 50 bps, 10-year yields sit at 5.13% and Brent is above $98. The AI trade gets two tests in 48 hours: Nvidia's guide on Tuesday and Anthropic's pricing on Wednesday. Then the consumer gets its turn. Here is the macro read, day by day. Monday A quiet start, with China doing the talking. XPeng, Baidu, H World and KE Holdings cover Chinese autos, ad spending, hotels and housing in one morning. KE is the one I'd watch. It is the cleanest real-time read on whether property transactions have found a floor. Tyson Foods is the US name to watch. Protein prices are where households feel inflation after the gas pump. Listen for trade-down from beef to chicken and anything on restaurant demand. Tuesday The main event, twice over. Home Depot reports before the open, with consensus at $3.86 on $42.72 billion in revenue. The numbers matter less than the commentary. Housing turnover was already frozen when the Fed was cutting and now mortgage rates are heading the wrong way. The question for Ted Decker is whether big-ticket projects are getting pushed out again and what pros are saying about backlogs.

title: Silver futures decline for 3rd time in 4 sessions as dollar climbs.
body: Silver futures fell for the third time in four sessions on Friday, tracking toward their eighth down week in the past 12 and a 30.5% decline over that period. During the session, prices reached a high of $50.725 before dropping to $48.835, putting the contract on pace for its lowest close in more than 13 months. Market projections indicate a 35 million ounce silver deficit this year—the sixth consecutive shortfall, though smaller than last year's—as total demand is forecast to decrease 5% alongside a 21% drop in solar demand. Meanwhile, monthly producer prices rose 0.3%, slightly below the 0.4% expectation. A stronger U.S. dollar, higher longer-term Treasury yields and expectations for a December Fed rate hike added further pressure ahead of next week's Fed minutes and Monday's testimony from Kevin Warsh.

title: 10-Year Treasury yields climb 30 bps on week to top 5.15%.
body: U.S. 10-Year Treasury Note yields extended their move higher on Friday, pushing above 5.15% intraday to reach their highest levels since early October. The benchmark 10-Year yield rose two to three bps on the day and finished roughly 30 bps higher for the week, settling just below 5.15%. Weekly gains were driven by inflation commentary from Federal Reserve speakers, stronger CPI data and lukewarm demand across 3-Year, 10-Year and 30-Year Treasury auctions. Despite rising yields, interest rate volatility tracked lower into the weekend and ended down for the week. Looking ahead, market participants await retail sales data, 20-Year and 10-Year TIPS auctions and remarks from Fed Chair Warsh on Monday in San Francisco.

title: Grain futures snap multi-week losing streaks to close the week.
body: Grain markets ended the week higher as Corn, Soybean and Wheat futures all snapped multi-week losing streaks. Corn export sales reached a marketing-year high of 2.881 million metric tons, alongside a 303,000 metric ton flash sale to Mexico, while CONAB held Brazilian corn output steady at 148 million metric tons. Soybean export sales totaled 1.15 million metric tons with three flash sales to China, Vietnam and unknown destinations, and CONAB left Brazilian soybean production unchanged at 181.6 million metric tons. title: Will the Senate's BAAJA Bill Let AI Giants Outmuscle Utilities?
